title: Spiral / Retrieval Review
subtitle: Revisiting earlier content on a spaced schedule — done as a short discussion, not a silent worksheet, so you keep the memory benefit *and* build reasoning.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Roediger & Karpicke (testing effect) · Rohrer & Bjork (spacing & interleaving) · Bay-Williams & SanGiovanni, Figuring Out Fluency.

blocks.text: A short opener that brings back **previously learned** content on a **spaced schedule** — so it doesn’t fade — run as a brief discussion where students compare strategies, not a silent set of problems.

The research here is unusually strong. The **spacing effect** (revisiting material over time) and the **testing effect** (the act of recalling strengthens memory) are among the most robust findings in all of learning science. Spiral review is how you bank those gains — provided you keep the delivery discourse-rich.

blocks.title: Keep the purpose, upgrade the delivery

blocks.text: Spiraling is excellent. A *silent individual worksheet* as the daily delivery is what we’re moving away from — it hides thinking, spends our best minutes on quiet recall, and reinforces “math = doing procedures alone.” Same retrieval benefit, far higher value: have students do a few spiraled problems, then **compare and defend strategies with a partner**.

blocks.label: Strands of Mathematical Proficiency
items: Procedural fluency
Conceptual understanding
Strategic competence

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Build fluency from understanding
Elicit & use evidence of thinking
Facilitate meaningful discourse
**Post 3–4 spiraled problems** — a mix of recent and older content, ideally interleaved (different types, not all the same).
**Students work them** on paper or whiteboards — showing strategy, not just answers.
**Compare & defend.** “Turn and compare with a partner — did anyone do it a different way? Resolve any disagreements.”
**Surface & settle.** Briefly share a strategy or a disagreement that’s worth the whole class’s attention.

blocks.text: What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Students comparing and defending strategies
A mix of old and recent topics (interleaved)
Work shown, so reasoning is visible
Disagreements surfaced and resolved
Brief — it primes the lesson, not replaces it

no.title: We should not see
items: A silent worksheet with no discussion
Only answers checked (a “7 out of 10”)
All-same-type drill in one block
Speed/competition pressure
15+ minutes eaten before the lesson starts

blocks.text: Spiral review is not the enemy — the *silent-worksheet delivery* is. If students are quietly grinding 10 problems while you check answers, you’ve recreated the very culture the vision is trying to leave. Keep the spacing; add the talk.

items: **The partner-compare step** gives multilingual learners and quieter students a low-stakes place to process and rehearse.
**Interleaving** (mixing topics) helps all students learn to choose strategies, not just repeat one — that’s real fluency.
**Showing work** lets you spot *where* a student’s reasoning breaks and respond, instead of only seeing right/wrong.

sections.label: Lesson design connection
sections.sources: Sources: Roediger & Karpicke (testing effect) · Rohrer & Bjork (spacing & interleaving) · Bay-Williams & SanGiovanni, Figuring Out Fluency.

blocks.text: Where it lives in the lesson
An **Opener routine** — reach for it when your purpose is to keep **previously taught content from fading**, or to warm up a prerequisite skill the day’s lesson needs.

Choose Spiral Review when the goal is durability and transfer rather than building a new idea. It’s also the honest home for the practice volume that fluency requires — just delivered as a short discussion, not a silent grind.

blocks.title: This is where “we need practice somehow” lives

blocks.text: Fluency needs reps, and the opener can carry some of them — as long as the reps come with talk. Do a few problems, then “compare with a partner.” You get the spacing and retrieval benefit *and* visible reasoning, which a silent worksheet never gives you.

items: **Mix recent + older.** A couple of problems from last week, one or two from a month ago — spacing is the point.
**Interleave types.** Don’t do 4 of the same; mixing forces students to decide *which* strategy applies, which is the heart of fluency.
**Target known weak spots** — the skills your formative evidence says are slipping.
**Sometimes seed the day:** include a prerequisite the new lesson depends on.

blocks.text: Turning a worksheet into a conversation

rows: 3–4 problems, then “compare your strategy with a partner — did anyone do it differently?”
Interleave: a fraction, an integer, a percent, a ratio
“Whose strategy was most efficient here? When would you use each?”
Self-paced; then a 2-minute “what tripped people up?” debrief

blocks.title: If you use a quiz tool (Quizizz, etc.)

blocks.text: Fine as a *delivery* mechanism — but configure it well: self-paced (not the live speed race), timer off or generous, explanations on, and **always debrief**. Better yet, have students show work on paper while you circulate, so you see *where* reasoning breaks — never just a score.

items: **Partner-compare** gives every student a place to process before any public sharing.
**Choose entry-friendly numbers** on at least one problem so every student starts with a success.
**Showing work** lets you respond to a student’s specific misconception in the moment — the monitoring that makes practice worthwhile.

blocks.text: The same purpose — durable, transferable fluency — carries into **Practice & Closure**, where distributed practice lives across the lesson and the week. Spiral Review is the opener-sized dose; the rest of the practice volume belongs in that component.
